## 📌 About
This project automatically fetches the latest papers from **arXiv** based on predefined keywords.
- Each section in the README corresponds to a **search keyword** (up to **20 per keyword**).
- The full list (up to **80 per keyword**) is available in the [`papers/`](papers/) directory.
- Click **Watch** (👀) on the repo to get **daily email notifications**.

_Last update: 2026-11-24_

| **[Task-Agnostic Incremental Vision-Language Object Detection via Prompt Augmentation and Distribution-Aware Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28291v1)** | 2026-11-20 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Incremental Vision-Language Object Detection (IVLOD) empowers pre-trained open-vocabulary detectors to continuously learn new visual concepts from sequential tasks without forgetting foundational knowledge. However, existing methods predominantly rely on oracle task identities during inference, severely limiting their open-world practicality. In this paper, we formalize Task-Agnostic IVLOD (TA-IVLOD), a more realistic setting where such priors are unavailable, requiring the model to simultaneously recognize classes from all learned tasks. This unconstrained setting exposes severe performance degradation due to cross-task semantic interference and parameter conflicts. To tackle these challenges, we propose TADA, a novel modular framework. Specifically, TADA introduces Stochastic Prompt Augmentation to mitigate semantic interference via training-time noise injection, and Test-Time Distribution-Aware Fusion to dynamically weight class-specific LoRA experts, effectively resolving parameter conflicts. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms baselines in standard IVLOD and yields substantial improvements in the rigorous TA-IVLOD setting on the ODinW-13 benchmark, while effectively preserving zero-shot generalization on the MS COCO dataset. The code is available at https://github.com/yonghanjiang/TADA.</p></details> |  |
| **[A Dynamical Theory of LoRA in Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39367v2)** | 2026-11-20 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Despite the widespread use of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), little is known about its dynamics in continual learning and the mechanisms by which low-rank updates affect catastrophic forgetting. We provide an asymptotically exact dynamical characterization of LoRA in a solvable two-task teacher-student model. In the high-dimensional online-learning limit, we derive a closed system of ordinary differential equations for a finite set of macroscopic order parameters, yielding exact expressions for the generalization errors throughout both the initial Task 1 learning phase and the subsequent LoRA fine-tuning on Task 2. The theory quantitatively matches finite-dimensional simulations and exposes two characteristic effects of LoRA: when the first-task representation is not yet specialized, low-rank adaptation reduces interference with features learned on the first task, but its initialization slows adaptation to the second task. Building on this mechanistic picture, we analyze a state-dependent masking strategy that freezes hidden units carrying the strongest first-task representations and restricts adaptation to the complementary subspace. This structural partitioning markedly reduces forgetting, while preserving plasticity on the new task. Our framework further clarifies the role of adapter rank: transfer improves only up to the intrinsic dimensionality of the target task and saturates beyond it, while forgetting continues to grow with rank. These results provide a dynamical and geometric account of how low-rank adaptation organizes information across sequential tasks, and are qualitatively reproduced on sequential MNIST and CIFAR-100 using a shallow network and ResNet-18, respectively.</p></details> | <details><summary>v2: a...</summary><p>v2: added a deep multi-task benchmark (ResNet-18, Split CIFAR-100), random-selection controls, a rank sweep at a fixed number of frozen units, and a deeper analysis of the specialized regime</p></details> |
| **[AlphaWiSE: Adaptive Weight Interpolation for Continual Multimodal Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15094v2)** | 2026-11-20 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Multimodal retrieval models align audio, images, and text in a shared embedding space, but sequential adaptation can degrade cross-modal relationships learned in earlier phases. Existing continual-learning procedures produce a single final checkpoint, so every retrieval direction shares the same stability-plasticity trade-off. We introduce AlphaWiSE, a post-hoc weight-space interpolation method that combines a sequential fine-tuning endpoint with a companion endpoint obtained with a stability-oriented continual-learning method. AlphaWiSE fits one scalar interpolation coefficient for each corresponding parameter tensor on an exemplar memory while both endpoints remain frozen. The interpolated tensors are then materialized into a single checkpoint, so the deployed model retains the architecture and inference cost of a single backbone. On continual audio-image-text retrieval, the fused model improves on the better of its two endpoints in 13 of 18 average retrieval measures and on the fixed blend of the same checkpoints in 25 of 36 measures. Its pairings achieve the strongest average audio-to-text and image-to-audio retrieval among all compared methods. Project page: https://alphawise.cvmlgroup.web.illinois.edu/</p></details> | <details><summary>Accep...</summary><p>Accepted to TMLR. Project page: https://alphawise.cvmlgroup.web.illinois.edu/</p></details> |
| **[From Acting to Learning: Experience Selection toward Continually Learning Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27159v1)** | 2026-11-20 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Successful agent interactions provide training data, but success alone does not determine which records a student should learn from. We examine experience selection for a 4B language agent as a component of continual agent learning. Nine selectors are compared across two fixed experience pools, eight initialization seeds, and two sampling seeds, yielding 288 trained students. Each student is evaluated on 128 development task groups with a common executor. With equal global selection freedom, 256 distinct contents, and 768 training presentations, optimizer-aware gradient selection reaches 81.45\% and 73.19\% success in the two pools. Its gains over global random selection are 8.25 and 5.96 percentage points; gains over global high-NLL selection are 4.10 and 4.05 points. All eight initialization-level contrasts are positive against both baselines in each pool. Relaxing coverage constraints improves gradient selection but reduces random-selection performance, showing that the ranking rule and selection space must be considered together. A separately frozen replication on 128 reserved task groups is complete; its equal-source gradient-minus-random and gradient-minus-high-NLL differences are +7.03 and +5.03 points, respectively.</p></details> |  |
| **[AhaBench: Do Agents Turn Experience into Reusable Insights? A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05435v3)** | 2026-11-20 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Solving a task, even from a worked example, does not make an agent any better at the next one. As agents move from single tasks to long collaborations with people, turning experience into reusable insight becomes the capability that separates a tool from a collaborator that improves over time. AhaBench is a benchmark for this kind of continual learning. It simulates three patterns of long human-AI collaboration and holds a later test fixed while varying the experience before it: in Aha-Puzzle, the agent questions a partner who knows the answer to a new mystery after solving earlier ones; in Aha-Euler, a person teaches a computation and the agent applies it to new inputs; in Aha-Vending, the agent runs a delegated business for a simulated year. The learning mechanism is left open, so memories, skill libraries, and weight updates can be compared under common rules against a baseline of fixed-weight agents that see their experience in context. Our results show that today's frontier agents are not yet continual learners. Earlier Aha-Puzzle solutions help some models, most clearly Qwen 3.6 Plus, which gains +12.57 points over attempts on the same stories without earlier episodes, yet every model scores far below what it reaches with hints. On single-step Aha-Euler tasks, the same model solves 94.0% of requested held-out inputs when taught with an explanation and code but 6.0% when given only the question and answer, counting unanswered attempts as incorrect. In incident-free Aha-Vending operation, Doubao Seed 2.0 Pro ends the year at +495 USD, yet its profit averaged over the year is -10 USD because it recovers late. Exploring without help, reconstructing a method, and sustaining productive operation remain open problems, and AhaBench provides the paired tests a learning method must pass to solve them.</p></details> | 35 pages, 8 figures |
| **[Task-Specific Agent Memory For Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29144v2)** | 2026-11-20 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Language-model agents can learn continually by storing useful instructions in memory and reusing them as new tasks arrive, without changing model weights. This requires both learning from new feedback and retaining earlier gains. However, an instruction learned from one task family can hurt other families when the agent uses the same memory for every task. We introduce task-specific agent memory: proposed skills are checked with execution tests, stored by task family, and retrieved for tasks in that family. We evaluate this design on a 12-round code-repair benchmark with recurring task families, tracking performance throughout learning. Holding proposals, acceptance decisions, and task completions fixed, task-specific retrieval raises average performance from 0.713 to 0.816. Across 27 paired randomized-order streams with Qwen3-Coder-Next, it improves average performance by 0.063 over global memory and by 0.055 over an agent that never updates its memory, accumulating 63 skills with no observed harmful acceptance. Capacity-matched retrieval and cumulative one-shot controls further support the value of task-specific retrieval and sequential skill accumulation. Our contribution is to identify cross-family interference and show how task-specific agent memory supports continual learning through skill accumulation and retention.</p></details> |  |
| **[Audit Before You Merge: Provenance, Probing, and Continual LoRA Composition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10684v2)** | 2026-11-19 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Post-hoc merging of public LoRA adapters is an attractive gradient-free path to continual adaptation, but reliable measurement of catastrophic forgetting in this setting depends on infrastructure that prior work has not addressed. We treat each adapter merge as a sequential task in a continual-learning setting, with the instruction-tuned base model's capabilities as Task 0, and study forgetting on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Public adapter hubs contain modules that fail basic provenance checks: silent base-version mismatches and near-zero delta norms whose inclusion inflates measured interference by ~10pp. We propose a two-check audit (base-model match, non-trivial delta norm) and a leakage-free probing protocol as preconditions for any forgetting study in this setting. On an audited 4-adapter set, naive merging causes -10.5pp on GSM8K and -18.3pp on HumanEval, while Task Arithmetic at lambda=0.5 sits within a standard error of the unmerged baseline. A coordinate search including negative coefficients identifies the math adapter as probe-optimal at lambda=-0.5, outside the reach of positive-only mergers, suggesting forgetting has structure that negation-aware merging may exploit. The same protocol replicates on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, where 2 of 4 candidate adapters fail the audit and the audited merge reproduces the same merge-method ranking on GSM8K, supporting that our findings are not Llama-specific.</p></details> | <details><summary>16 pa...</summary><p>16 pages, 4 figures, 17 tables. ICML 2026 Workshop on Continual Adaptation at Scale (CATS). Code: https://github.com/LennyAharon/audit_continual_learning v2: corrected references</p></details> |
| **[Homeostatic Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13771v2)** | 2026-11-19 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>I formulate a Continual Learning problem for an autonomous agent that imitates the one animals face. The agent has intents to satisfy. It experiences contexts where different combinations of features are active and impact intent outcomes. I propose a method named ``Homeostatic Continual Learning'' that imitates the one animals use. The agent learns incrementally environment data and features relevant for their intents from the impact of contexts, gradually completes its model and policy and performs well in more and more contexts. The core of the method is to find outliers in the environment data when the agent experiences an outlier in its intent outcome after the context changes. This method enables the agent to learn continuously in changing contexts without catastrophic forgetting. When pursuing many intents concurrently, the agent may build a transformer-like world model with the method where it factorizes the objects in the world into features, abstract objects into comparable instances of concepts and map concepts to intents through features. The world model is composed of semantic nodes and explainable by nature. I discuss the works needed to render the method practical, the connections to many fields in Artificial Intelligence and the broader implications of the method.</p></details> | <details><summary>19 pa...</summary><p>19 pages, 13 figures, 1 table</p></details> |
| **[Policy Improvement-Guided Replay for Continual Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25989v1)** | 2026-11-19 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires models to acquire new capabilities while retaining performance on previous tasks. A stability-oriented perspective common in conventional continual learning emphasizes knowledge preservation and interference mitigation. Complementing this perspective, we revisit CRL for vision-language models through policy improvement, a fundamental principle of RL, to preserve acquired performance gains. Using the performance difference lemma, we characterize historical performance changes through the current policy's expected advantages on historical task distributions, motivating replay of historical prompts with the current policy. To allocate limited replay memory, we propose Contrastive Likelihood Replay (CoLiR), which contrasts likelihood gains on correct responses from the final task policy with likelihood reductions on incorrect responses from the initial policy. Our analysis links correct-response likelihood gains to reference-policy advantages under an idealized KL-regularized optimal update and provides an endogenous-reward interpretation for general policy updates. CoLiR estimates scores from finite training rollouts and cached log-likelihoods, selects prompts at task boundaries, and replays them uniformly during subsequent training, with KL regularization restricted to replayed prompts. Memory construction only requires a small amount of additional cross-policy scoring but no additional response generation. Across three Qwen3-VL model sizes on MRCL, CoLiR achieves the highest mean final accuracy and mean task accuracy among the compared methods while maintaining competitive new-task performance.</p></details> |  |
| **[HOPD: Historical On-Policy Distillation for SAR MLLM Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25391v1)** | 2026-11-19 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Continual SAR interpretation requires multimodal large language models to learn incoming sources while retaining earlier task abilities. This is difficult when acquisition and geographic shifts alter visual evidence, regionally concentrated categories bias answers, and historical images are scarce. We address this problem with Historical On-Policy Distillation (HOPD), which reuses source-acquisition LoRA states as persistent teachers for one evolving student. Archiving each state before consolidation preserves a stable source reference. The teachers supervise student-generated prefixes, transferring historical behavior to the student's changing generation contexts. To enrich sparse replay, original-view teachers guide augmented historical student views while preserving spatial coordinates. This knowledge is consolidated into a single deployed adapter that requires no source identity. On SARVQA-CL, our source-incremental evaluation protocol, HOPD achieves the highest final mean score of 54.51 among the compared methods, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.96 points. It also improves the final source-macro score in every evaluated task over shared-memory Replay-SFT, with gains across source orders. These results support source-acquisition history as supervision for retaining earlier task performance during continual SAR adaptation. Code and data: https://github.com/zcablii/HOPD.</p></details> |  |
| **[Some Memories Must Fade: Persistence and Decay of User Memories in Model Parameters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25235v1)** | 2026-11-18 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.</p></details> | 30 pages, 8 figures |
| **[Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24637v1)** | 2026-11-18 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.</p></details> |  |
| **[PoCoFL: A Framework for POlicy-COmpliant Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03650v2)** | 2026-11-18 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Federated Learning (FL) is a privacy-oriented learning paradigm that enables collaborative model training while keeping training data local to clients. However, FL does not guarantee that clients submit policy-compliant contributions or that aggregators process admitted contributions correctly. Update-magnitude bounds alone cannot ensure compliance with learning-specific requirements involving private data, intermediate models, or retained state. These requirements differ across FL settings, motivating a unified framework to specify and verify client and aggregation policies. This work introduces PoCoFL, a policy-compliant federated learning framework that separates three aspects: (i) FL type, (ii) policy semantics, and (iii) cryptographic realisation. We provide a formalisation that captures client and aggregation requirements as policy-dependent relations, defining update admissibility, aggregation correctness, and policy-relative privacy. These relations enable verification of selected properties of intermediate objects, such as local-model loss, continual-learning state, and personalised optimisation conditions, in each round. Clients demonstrate compliance of their contributions using compatible cryptographic mechanisms, while aggregators prove that the recorded set of admitted contributions was processed according to the selected aggregation policy. We demonstrate PoCoFL through four formal instantiations and corresponding proof-of-concept realisations: (i) vanilla, (ii) continual, (iii) personalised, and (iv) threshold-encrypted federated learning. We evaluate how policy enforcement affects the learning objectives of vanilla, personalised, and continual FL, and quantify the computational and communication overhead of policy verification across all four instantiations. These results demonstrate that PoCoFL captures complex policy representations across the evaluated FL settings.</p></details> |  |
| **[Learning with Unlearning: Synaptic Role Partitioning for Simultaneous Continual Learning and Machine Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24205v1)** | 2026-11-18 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Continual Learning (CL) asks a model to acquire new knowledge without forgetting what it already knows. Machine Unlearning (MU) asks it to destroy specific knowledge without damaging the rest. The challenge is integrating them in the same system; the two objectives pull on the same weights, and an edit made for one harms the other. To address this, we propose Learning with Unlearning (LwU), a unified framework that resolves the conflict where it occurs: at the individual synapse. LwU scores every weight twice, once against the data to keep and once against the data to delete, and partitions the network into four zones with separate update rules. Weights that only require retention are frozen. Weights that only require deletion are cleared and returned to the network as free capacity. Contested weights take a gradient-ascent step projected orthogonally to the retention gradient. The remaining capacity learns the incoming task by a privileged teacher via self-distillation. Deletion is served post hoc, and no retraining is required. Across both CL and MU jobs, LwU outperforms or matches the strongest baseline. Its real-world practicality has been demonstrated on the Physical Artificial Intelligence (PAI) dataset we conducted. Additionally, in the image generation task and in removing dangerous content, it outperformed the closest baseline, as shown in Fig.1.</p></details> |  |
| **[UCLIR: Unsupervised Continual Learning using Independent Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24093v1)** | 2026-11-18 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>In continual learning, regularization-based methods aim to mimic neuroplasticity by updating network weights to learn new tasks while constraining changes to parameters that are important for previously learned tasks through penalty terms. However, as the number of tasks increases, preserving knowledge from earlier tasks becomes less effective. This is mainly because updates for new tasks are distributed across the entire network, where parameters are highly interdependent due to the dense connectivity between neurons. Inspired by the Exponential Distance Rule (EDR), which states that the number of neural connections decreases with increasing physical distance, learning is naturally locally correlated while inter-area updates remain less task-dependent. Motivated by this principle, in this paper we demonstrate that applying weight regularization to multiple small and independently learned complementary representations is more effective than regularizing a single large shared representation. By decomposing the input into independently learned components, learning new tasks induces only localized parameter updates within specific representation, which limit interference and improve knowledge retention across tasks. We employ independent autoencoders that learn different parts of the input independently through unsupervised regularization. At inference time, a linear classifier is used for evaluation. The experimental results on a sequence of tasks using 5-Splits MNIST, sequence of 5-datasets, 5-Splits CIFAR-10, 10-Splits Tiny ImageNet shows competitive results with supervised and replay-based methods. Code is available.</p></details> |  |
| **[MIST: Reliable Streaming Decision Trees for Online Class-Incremental Learning via McDiarmid Bound](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11617v3)** | 2026-11-18 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Streaming decision trees are natural candidates for open-world continual learning, as they perform local updates, enjoy bounded memory, and static decision boundaries. Despite these, they still fail in online class-incremental learning due to two coupled miscalibrations: (i) their split criterion grows unreliable as the class count K expands, and (ii) the absence of knowledge transfer at split time. Both failures share a common root: the range of Information Gain intrinsically scales with log2 K. Consequently, any Hoeffding-style confidence radius derived from it must inevitably grow with the class count, making a K-independent split criterion structurally impossible, taking away the potential benefits of applying streaming decision trees to continual learning. To fix this issue, we present MIST (McDiarmid Incremental Streaming Tree), which resolves both failures through three integrated components: (i) a tight, K-independent McDiarmid confidence radius for Gini splitting that acts as a structural regulariser; (ii) a Bayesian inheritance protocol that projects parent statistics to child nodes via truncated-Gaussian moments, with variance reduction guarantees strongest precisely when splitting is most conservative; and (iii) per-leaf KLL quantile sketches that support both continuous threshold evaluation and geometry-adaptive leaf prediction from a single data structure. On standard and stress-test tabular streams, MIST is competitive with global parametric methods on near-Gaussian benchmarks and uniquely robust on non-Gaussian geometry where SOTA benchmarks collapse.</p></details> | <details><summary>Accep...</summary><p>Accepted At Neurips 2026</p></details> |
| **[GaussLearner: 3D Gaussian Primitives as Self-Regulating Continual Learners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23736v1)** | 2026-11-18 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Continual learning of 3D Gaussian fields aims to maintain faithful reconstructions of the evolving world. However, directly fine-tuning an existing Gaussian field on new observations can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously reconstructed content. To address this challenge, existing methods employ selective local optimization, replay, or parameter regularization, yet still struggle to balance adaptation to scene changes with preservation of still-valid content. Our key insight is to view 3D Gaussian primitives themselves as self-regulating continual learners. Based on this insight, we introduce GaussLearner, which equips each Gaussian with a closed continual-learning loop connecting observation, self-regulation, and adaptation at the primitive level. At each novel state, GaussLearner first attributes pixel-wise inconsistencies in current observations to their contributing Gaussians. Each Gaussian then self-regulates through a learning weight that balances current observations against cross-state reliability. This weight governs both Gaussian parameter adaptation and optimizer memory refresh. As current inconsistencies are resolved, the adaptation outcome renews each Gaussian's reliability for future states. The resulting field is a globally coupled population of locally self-regulating learners. Across scenes from CL-Splats, WAT, and our CL-3D dataset, GaussLearner improves average PSNR by 3.41 dB over the strongest baseline. On CL-3D, it achieves the best reconstruction quality on both changed and unchanged views.</p></details> | <details><summary>Proje...</summary><p>Project Page: https://gaoxiang-linghu.github.io/GaussLearner/</p></details> |
| **[DuoCL: Dual-Path Online Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23598v1)** | 2026-11-17 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Online continual learning (OCL) requires learning from a data stream whose arrival rate is independent of model training speed. When training cannot keep pace, computationally expensive gradient-based methods update less frequently, limiting adaptation. Analytic methods reduce this overhead, but their frozen backbones cannot adapt representations to changing distributions. We propose DuoCL, a dual-path OCL framework whose fast analytic path accumulates feature statistics from every incoming minibatch while its slow path periodically adapts the backbone. The slow path adjusts its sample count to the available compute budget without interrupting fast-path learning. Feature alignment compensates for drift in the accumulated classifier statistics. Across four datasets and three computational budgets, DuoCL improves online accuracy by an average of 9.67 percentage points over the strongest gradient-based baseline in each setting. DuoCL consistently outperforms analytic learning under distribution shifts, with gains of up to 4.00 percentage points on CIFAR-C, and achieves higher accuracy than prior methods across disjoint class-incremental, domain-incremental, and Si-Blurry settings.</p></details> | Technical Report |
| **[FedRAN: Accurate and Efficient Analytic Federated Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11480v2)** | 2026-11-17 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Federated continual learning (FCL) enables distributed clients to learn from evolving data streams while retaining knowledge from previously observed tasks. Existing optimization-based FCL methods often rely on repeated local training, incurring communication overhead and feature drift across clients. Analytic alternatives avoid iterative training, but high-dimensional random features used to improve accuracy require communicating a Gram matrix whose cost grows quadratically with feature dimension. Communication-efficient alternatives reduce this cost by statistically reconstructing the Gram matrix from first-order summaries. We propose FedRAN, a low-rank analytic FCL framework that instead compresses the required second-order structure directly through spectral summaries that are merged across clients and tasks. The retained rank explicitly controls the tradeoff between approximation fidelity and communication, reducing second-order communication from quadratic to linear in feature dimension for a fixed rank. Objects in dynamic motion remain a significant challenge for dense visual SLAM since dynamic observations can contaminate camera tracking and scene reconstruction. Although 3DGS (3D Gaussian splatting) enables efficient dense mapping, existing 3DGS-SLAM systems may exhibit instability when dynamic objects violate their underlying static-scene assumption. Excluding dynamic observations can reduce their influence on tracking and mapping, but may leave occluded static backgrounds missing or weakly constrained. Dynamic regions are identified through optical-flow-based motion discovery and temporally consistent mask propagation by SAM2. For selected keyframes, a fine-tuned diffusion inpainting model generates plausible background appearance in occluded regions, while metric depth predicted from completed images initializes provisional Gaussian primitives. Provenance labels distinguish generated primitives from observation-supported primitives, excluding generated content from camera-pose estimation and observed-map optimization. When previously occluded backgrounds become visible, eligible generated primitives are removed, and observation-supported primitives are independently initialized from real RGB observations and predicted depth. Additionally, we demonstrate DynoSAM utility in downstream applications, including 3D reconstruction of dynamic scenes and trajectory prediction, thereby showcasing potential for advancing dynamic object-aware SLAM systems. | **[MLP-SLAM: Multilayer Perceptron-Based Simultaneous Localization and Mapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10669v2)** | 2025-11-06 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>The Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (V-SLAM) system has seen significant development in recent years, demonstrating high precision in environments with limited dynamic objects. Existing solutions address this by continuously introducing additional line and plane features to supplement point features, achieving robust tracking and pose estimation. However, current methods continuously introduce additional features regardless of necessity, causing two problems: unnecessary computational overhead and potential performance degradation from accumulated low-quality additional features and noise. To address these issues, this paper proposes a feature-aware mechanism that evaluates whether current features are adequate to determine if line feature support should be activated. This decision mechanism enables the system to introduce line features only when necessary, significantly reducing computational complexity of additional features while minimizing the introduction of low-quality features and noise. In subsequent processing, the introduced line features assist in obtaining better initial camera poses through tracking, local mapping, and loop closure, but are excluded from global optimization to avoid potential negative impacts from low-quality additional features in long-term process. Extensive experiments on TUM datasets demonstrate substantial improvements in both ATE and RPE metrics compared to ORB-SLAM3 baseline and superior performance over other dynamic SLAM and multi-feature methods.</p></details> | <details><summary>submi...</summary><p>submitted to International Conference on Robotic Computing and Communication(IEEE IRC)</p></details> |

| **[GARAD-SLAM: 3D GAussian splatting for Real-time Anti Dynamic SLAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03228v2)** | 2025-02-18 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>The 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based SLAM system has garnered widespread attention due to its excellent performance in real-time high-fidelity rendering. | **[EndoS3:Endoscopic Semantic Splatting SLAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04358v1)** | 2026-11-03 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Purpose: Despite advances in 3D surgical scene understanding, semantic simultaneous localisation and mapping (SLAM) remains under-explored for two key reasons. A semantic node allocation module redistributes a fixed node budget across instances according to their size and non-rigidity. We evaluate the approach on well-known benchmarks and custom datasets specifically designed for assistive navigation scenarios. | **[SlideSLAM: Sparse, Lightweight, Decentralized Metric-Semantic SLAM for Multi-Robot Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17249v7)** | 2025-10-03 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>This paper develops a real-time decentralized metric-semantic SLAM algorithm that enables a heterogeneous robot team to collaboratively construct object-based metric-semantic maps. | **[Semantic Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping: A Survey on State of the Art, Challenges, and Future Directions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00783v1)** | 2025-10-01 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Semantic Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is a critical area of research within robotics and computer vision, focusing on the simultaneous localization of robotic systems and associating semantic information to construct the most accurate and complete comprehensive model of the surrounding environment. Since the first foundational work in Semantic SLAM appeared more than two decades ago, this field has received increasing attention across various scientific communities. Despite its significance, the field lacks comprehensive surveys encompassing recent advances and persistent challenges. In response, this study provides a thorough examination of the state-of-the-art of Semantic SLAM techniques, with the aim of illuminating current trends and key obstacles. Beginning with an in-depth exploration of the evolution of visual SLAM, this study outlines its strengths and unique characteristics, while also critically assessing previous survey literature. Subsequently, a unified problem formulation and evaluation of the modular solution framework is proposed, which divides the problem into discrete stages, including visual localization, semantic feature extraction, mapping, data association, and loop closure optimization. Moreover, this study investigates alternative methodologies such as deep learning and the utilization of large language models, alongside a review of relevant research about contemporary SLAM datasets. Concluding with a discussion on potential future research directions, this study serves as a comprehensive resource for researchers seeking to navigate the complex landscape of Semantic SLAM.</p></details> |  |
| **[Human Interaction for Collaborative Semantic SLAM using Extended Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14949v1)** | 2025-09-18 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Semantic SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) systems enrich robot maps with structural and semantic information, enabling robots to operate more effectively in complex environments. However, these systems struggle in real-world scenarios with occlusions, incomplete data, or ambiguous geometries, as they cannot fully leverage the higher-level spatial and semantic knowledge humans naturally apply. We introduce HICS-SLAM, a Human-in-the-Loop semantic SLAM framework that uses a shared extended reality environment for real-time collaboration. The system allows human operators to directly interact with and visualize the robot's 3D scene graph, and add high-level semantic concepts (e.g., rooms or structural entities) into the mapping process. We propose a graph-based semantic fusion methodology that integrates these human interventions with robot perception, enabling scalable collaboration for enhanced situational awareness. Experimental evaluations on real-world construction site datasets demonstrate improvements in room detection accuracy, map precision, and semantic completeness compared to automated baselines, demonstrating both the effectiveness of the approach and its potential for future extensions.</p></details> | <details><summary>7 pag...</summary><p>7 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables</p></details> |

| **[PRIMA: Preference-Informed Multimodal Trajectory Planning with Vision-Language Model for Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.04209v3)** | 2026-11-22 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Decision-making and motion planning constitute critical components for ensuring the safety and efficiency of autonomous vehicles (AVs). Existing methodologies typically adopt two paradigms: decision then planning or generation then scoring. However, the former architecture often suffers from decision-planning misalignment that incurs risky situations. Meanwhile, the latter struggles to balance short-term operational metrics (e.g., immediate motion smoothness) with long-term tactical goals (e.g., route efficiency), resulting in myopic or overly conservative behaviors. To address these issues, we introduce PRIMA, a preference-informed multimodal trajectory planning framework assisted by a Vision-Language Model (VLM). Our approach employs a tri-stage cognitive decomposition protocol, encompassing scene understanding, action selection, and confidence assessment, to generate diverse candidate actions paired with verbalized confidence scores. This reasoning mechanism exposes alternative tactical choices and provides an empirical preference signal for balancing them with downstream planning quality. Furthermore, we propose a novel planning module that integrates a diffusion model for trajectory generation and a hierarchical refinement process to find the optimal trajectory. This enables the selection over trajectory candidates accounting for both low-level solution quality and high-level tactical preferences, avoiding the risks within one-shot decisions and overcoming the limitations of short-sighted scoring mechanisms. Comprehensive simulation-based closed-loop evaluations on nuPlan and InterPlan demonstrate competitive performance across common and long-tail benchmarks. A paired controlled intervention further evaluates the incremental decision utility of the verbalized confidence signal. The code will be released upon acceptance.</p></details> | 14 pages, 9 figures |
| **[MoT3DVG: A Benchmark for Outdoor 3D Visual Grounding with Motion-Aware Descriptions and Temporal Cues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11334v2)** | 2026-11-22 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>3D visual grounding (3DVG) localizes language-referred objects in 3D scenes, with broad applicability in both indoor and outdoor environments. We therefore introduce MoT3DVG, a large-scale dataset for dynamic-aware outdoor 3DVG with temporally evolving motion descriptions. It contains 850 scenarios with 31,128 frames from nuScenes dataset, and provides 144,568 language prompts with motion-aware descriptions for dynamic objects across time. We further propose DynaVG, a novel framework that effectively leverages temporal cues for outdoor 3DVG. In addition to the standard modality-specific encoders, DynaVG introduces a Short-Long Integrated Dynamic Encoding (SLIDE) module before the language-point cloud alignment. SLIDE models both local motion cues and global temporal context via short-term window encoding and long-term window shifting. Extensive experiments demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG, validating the effectiveness of motion-aware encoding. | **[Your Diffusion-Based Driving Planner Only Needs a Nudge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29123v1)** | 2026-11-22 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Diffusion-based planners capture the multimodality of human driving behavior well, yet covariate shift in closed-loop driving can lead them to generate trajectories that result in collisions or road departures. Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning offers a promising way to tackle this issue, but applying it to diffusion-based planners is complicated by their iterative denoising process and receding-horizon execution. We find that small adjustments to the planned trajectories can prevent many of these unsafe outcomes. Motivated by this observation, we propose PlanNudge, which preserves the learned planning capabilities of a pretrained diffusion-based planner by freezing it and trains a lightweight policy that we call the nudge policy. At each planning step, the nudge policy outputs a nudge, a two-dimensional adjustment of the speed and curvature of the plan from the frozen planner. The nudge policy is a multilayer perceptron that predicts the nudge in a single forward pass, and both dimensions directly change the motion of the vehicle, so standard off-policy RL can train it in closed-loop simulation. We evaluate PlanNudge on nuPlan, a large-scale autonomous driving benchmark based on real-world driving data. In all six settings, PlanNudge matches or exceeds the final scores of the previous state-of-the-art RL finetuning method while using about one sixth as many environment steps and less than one fifth as much model compute. We also provide guidelines for reward shaping, value learning, and exploration when using off-policy RL to post-train autonomous driving planners. Our results are reported with means and standard deviations over six training runs. Project page: https://zerlinwang.github.io/plannudge/</p></details> | <details><summary>Auton...</summary><p>Autonomous driving, Trajectory Planning, Diffusion-based Planners, Reinforcement Learning, RL Post-training, Off-policy RL</p></details> |
| **[CP-Guard+: A New Paradigm for Malicious Agent Detection and Defense in Multi-Agent Collaborative Perception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.07807v3)** | 2026-11-21 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Collaborative perception (CP) is a promising approach for safe connected and autonomous driving that enables multiple connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) to share sensing information with each other to enhance perception performance. Furthermore, we develop a robust defense method called CP-Guard+, which enhances the margin between the representations of benign and malicious features through a carefully designed dual-centered contrastive loss. While existing models of private AV sharing often take ownership as given, in this paper, we develop a stationary equilibrium model in which vehicle ownership and listing decisions determine service availability and operational frictions, which in turn shape individuals' incentives to own and share. Based on the model, we first characterize individual choices by comparing payoffs of being an owner and a non-owner. We then analyze the resulting potential population partitions, establish conditions for the existence of an active sharing market, and categorize them by owner types. | **[Hybrid Adaptive Kalman Filtering for Data-Efficient Joint Tracking and Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.02767v2)** | 2026-11-21 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Kalman filtering performance is highly sensitive to model mismatch and noise covariance tuning. Classical adaptive filtering methods address these issues by estimating model parameters or noise covariances from measurement data but rely on a predefined model structure. Learning-based methods provide greater flexibility but typically require large supervised datasets and often lack well-calibrated uncertainty estimates. This article proposes a self-supervised Hybrid Adaptive Kalman Filter (HAKF) that learns time-varying corrections to the system dynamics and process-noise covariance directly from measurements while jointly estimating the measurement-noise covariance. Because these corrections are learned from measurements alone, we analyze the structural identifiability of the corresponding time-invariant parameterizations. For a constant-velocity model with position-only measurements, an unrestricted process-noise covariance is not identifiable even when the dynamics are known, whereas a physically structured parameterization that couples the dynamics and process covariance is jointly identifiable with the measurement-noise covariance. This analysis motivates a structured HAKF variant, compared with a flexible variant that adapts the dynamics and process covariance independently. The innovation likelihood of HAKF also enables model classification through generalized Bayesian inference. In Isaac Lab simulations, the structured HAKF improves tracking accuracy over a fitted Kalman filter across all training-set sizes. When training data are limited, its advantage over the flexible variant is largest, and it outperforms a supervised recurrent neural network in both tracking and classification. The identifier requires no policy training and thus applies to any frozen visuomotor policy. Since visual shifts remain visible to the policy, PEA further adapts the frozen policy with a removable low-rank adapter, addressing coupled visual and actuation shifts.
